summary.text: In DNA replication, a cell produces exact copies of its own DNA.
It is essential to inheritance, cell division and repair of damaged tissues, and gives each daughter cell its own copy of each DNA molecule.
The two strands separate and each one serves as a template for a new partner strand, so every new molecule keeps one original strand.

facts.label: Copy style
facts.value: Semiconservative: one old strand, one new strand

facts.label: Starting points
facts.value: Origins of replication, scattered across the genome

facts.label: Builder enzyme
facts.value: DNA polymerase adds nucleotides matching the template

items.prompt: A cell copies a double-stranded DNA molecule once. What does each resulting molecule contain?

options.label: Two original strands, with the copy built apart
One original strand and one newly made strand
Two newly made strands and no original strand
Half of each strand fused into one

items.explain: Each original strand serves as a template for a new partner, so every new molecule has one old and one new strand.

items.prompt: A lab wants a polymerase to start copying a template. Why can it not simply begin on bare DNA?

options.label: It can only extend an existing strand, so a short RNA primer goes first
It can only read RNA, so the DNA must be converted first
It works only on single nucleotides, so the DNA must be cut up first
It can only add to the 5' end, so a primer must be flipped around

items.explain: DNA polymerases cannot start new strands, only extend one, so a short RNA primer is paired with the template first.

items.prompt: Replication begins at one spot on the DNA. How do the replication forks grow from there?

options.label: In one direction only, toward the next origin
Only once the whole genome has been unwound
Inward, from the genome's ends toward the origin
In both directions away from the origin

items.explain: Unwinding at the origin makes replication forks that grow bi-directionally.

items.prompt: Why can the two strands be pulled apart for copying without breaking either strand?

options.label: Bonds along each strand are weaker than the bonds linking the two
The strands are held together only by the polymerase enzyme
Bonds linking the strands are weaker than the bonds along each strand
The nucleobases face outward, so the strands barely touch

items.explain: Phosphodiester bonds within a strand are stronger than the hydrogen bonds between strands, so the strands can separate.

items.prompt: A cell is in the S (synthesis) stage of interphase. What is its main job then?

options.label: Making a copy of its DNA
Splitting into two daughter cells
Reading mRNA to build proteins
Destroying its damaged DNA

items.explain: DNA replication occurs during the S stage of interphase.

items.prompt: A polymerase is building a new strand. Where does it attach each new nucleotide?

options.label: To the 5' end of the growing chain
To the 3' end of the growing chain
To the middle of the growing chain
Only at the origin of replication

items.explain: DNA polymerase can only synthesize by adding nucleotides to the 3' end of a strand.

paragraphs.heading: What it is
paragraphs.text: DNA replication is how a cell makes exact copies of its DNA. It happens in every living thing. Inheritance, cell division and the repair of damaged tissue all rely on it. When a cell divides, replication makes sure each newly formed daughter cell gets its own copy of every DNA molecule.

paragraphs.heading: Two strands that match
paragraphs.text: Most DNA has two strands that twist around each other into a double helix. Each strand is a chain of four kinds of nucleotides, the small units of DNA, and each nucleotide holds a sugar called deoxyribose, a phosphate and a base. The bases are adenine, cytosine, guanine and thymine, written A, C, G and T. Across the two strands, bases pair up through hydrogen bonds: A with T, and G with C. Because the strands match, the information in one is repeated in its partner.

paragraphs.heading: Copying by halves
paragraphs.text: To copy the molecule, the cell separates the two strands. Each old strand then acts as a template, a pattern for building a new matching strand. This is called semiconservative replication, since every finished molecule keeps one old strand and gains one new one. The strands can come apart because the hydrogen bonds between them are weaker than the phosphodiester bonds that hold each strand together along its length.

paragraphs.heading: Where and when it starts
paragraphs.text: Copying usually starts at particular spots called origins of replication, spread across the genome. There, enzymes called helicases unwind the DNA, opening replication forks that grow in both directions away from the origin. Many proteins gather at each fork to start the work and keep it going. In cells, all this takes place during the S, or synthesis, stage of interphase.

paragraphs.heading: The builder enzyme
paragraphs.text: The main builder is DNA polymerase, a family of enzymes that carry out every form of DNA replication. It adds nucleotides that match those on the template strand. It cannot start a new strand from nothing, though; it can only lengthen a strand already paired with the template. So a short piece of RNA called a primer has to be made first. Polymerase also works in one direction only, adding each new nucleotide to the 3′ end of the strand.

paragraphs.heading: Energy and accuracy
paragraphs.text: Each free nucleotide arrives with three phosphate groups attached. When it joins the chain, two of them break off together as pyrophosphate, and breaking that high-energy bond supplies the energy for the step. Splitting the pyrophosphate afterwards uses up a second such bond and makes the reaction effectively one-way. Polymerases are also very accurate, making fewer than one mistake per 10⁷ nucleotides added, and some can remove a wrongly matched nucleotide from the end of the growing strand.

paragraphs.heading: Copying in a test tube
paragraphs.text: Replication can also be done outside a cell. Scientists take DNA polymerases from cells and add artificial primers to begin copying at known sequences of a DNA template. The polymerase chain reaction, or PCR, is a common example of this technique.
